articles.title: Wu Shicun on why Beijing will not rule out Scarborough Shoal construction
articles.summary:
- Wu Shicun, founding president of China's National Institute for South China Sea Studies, describes the Philippines' "assertive transparency" campaign as a deliberate strategy since 2023 to provoke Chinese interceptions (water cannons, blockades) around Renai Jiao/Second Thomas Shoal, then package confrontations into viral videos to shape international opinion portraying China as the aggressor.

- He argues the Philippines' media-driven approach serves domestic political aims—securing increased budget and equipment support for its coastguard from Congress—while being amplified by Western media backing.

- China has focused its diplomatic capital on institutional rule-making, including over a decade of Code of Conduct (COC) negotiations since 2013 and the 56th working group session on implementing the Declaration on Conduct of Parties (DOC), rather than on narrative combat.

- Wu acknowledges China was initially caught off-guard during the 2023 Second Thomas Shoal stand-off and later incidents like Sabina Shoal intrusions, but has since adjusted its counter-strategy to proactively challenge and expose what he calls the Philippines' deliberate disinformation campaigns.

- Beijing is now shifting to a more proactive approach to construct its own South China Sea narrative, a paradigm change Wu frames as a lesson learned from countering Manila's playbook.

articles.title: Susan Thornton on US-China ties, post-midterms and averting a new balloon crisis
articles.summary:
- **Susan Thornton**, a former acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, calls US-China leader-level summits "the only guardrail" in the bilateral relationship, given the lack of other stabilizing mechanisms, and advocates for normalizing such high-level meetings.

- She argues that expectations for long lists of tangible outcomes at every summit are counterproductive, as they make regular meetings difficult to sustain and hold them to an unnecessarily higher bar.

- Thornton frames the goal of US-China engagement as achieving **"constructive strategic stability"**—primarily avoiding worst-case scenarios and crises that could escalate into conflict, citing examples like the 2023 spy balloon incident and Pelosi's 2022 Taiwan visit.

- She notes that Trump has experience managing US-China tensions from his first term, which ended poorly under COVID-19, but believes he has reflected on that period and better understands the dynamics that led to the breakdown.

- **President Trump's twice-repeated engagement with Xi Jinping** (in Beijing and Washington) may help regularize high-level meetings, which Thornton sees as essential for keeping the relationship on track.

articles.title: Zheng Yongnian on Trump, Venezuela and why China doesn’t want ‘a separate kitchen’
articles.summary:
• **Trump's strategic pivot ("Donroe Doctrine"):** Zheng Yongnian argues that Trump is shifting US strategy from global engagement to consolidating influence in the Western Hemisphere, combining the Monroe Doctrine with offshore balancing — a move he believes Trump can actually execute, unlike his predecessors. Trump views the presence of China and Russia in Latin America as a national security threat.

• **Global turbulence ahead:** Zheng predicts widespread disruption regardless of whether the US retreats from or advances into regions. US withdrawal from Europe, the Middle East, and East Asia — where its interests are deeply embedded — will create local chaos, while its re-embedding into Latin America could cause similar disruption.

• **Tripartite world partition discussion:** American right-wing think tanks have discussed a tripartite partition of the world, with Trump being the second major power leader to pursue this — after Vladimir Putin. Europe, particularly nations like Poland, fears that a US-Russia compromise over Ukraine would leave Ukraine as Russia's final target, not its only ambition.

• **Rise of "regional lords":** Beyond big-power dynamics, smaller regional powers such as Turkey in Turkic-speaking countries are asserting themselves, adding another layer of complexity to the shifting global order. Zheng emphasizes that big powers drive major geopolitical shifts, and Venezuela will not be the US's last intervention target in Latin America.

articles.title: Liu Qian on Chinese innovation, the US rivalry and women holding up half the sky
articles.summary:
Here is a concise summary of the article:

• **Trade concerns are exaggerated:** US exports make up only about 2.8% of China's GDP (exports account for ~19% of GDP total, with the US representing 14.7% of that). Even a complete loss of the US export market would impact only 2–3% of China's economy.

• **China's export portfolio has diversified significantly:** ASEAN is now China's largest export destination, and emerging markets are growing fast — exports to Brazil rose 23.3% last year, and exports to Africa grew 25.9% in the first eight months of this year.

• **Exporters have shown resilience:** Despite tariff pressures, Chinese exporters have adapted creatively by shifting routes, entering new markets, and adjusting products and packaging, keeping exports generally steady.

• **The US-China rivalry extends beyond trade:** It now encompasses technology, ideologies, and global collaboration, and Liu warns that continued unhealthy competition will harm both countries and the world.

• **Broader economic risks remain:** Potential impacts include unemployment affecting private consumption and social stability, business sentiment being clouded by uncertainty, and supply chains needing to restructure in response to shifting demand patterns.

articles.title: Fuchsia Dunlop tells how she fell for China’s cuisine and names her perfect dish
articles.summary:
• **Fuchsia Dunlop is a British author and chef widely regarded as the Western world's foremost expert on Chinese cuisine**, particularly Sichuanese food, having written seven books on the subject.

• **Dunlop discovered Chinese cuisine in 1994** while attending Sichuan University as a British Council postgraduate student in Chengdu; she persuaded local restaurant owners and the Sichuan Higher Institute of Cuisine to train her, completing a three-month chef's course with 50 Sichuanese students.

• **Her first Sichuan cookbook, published in 2001, filled a notable gap** in English-language culinary literature—she noted that despite Sichuan being the size of a European country, virtually no Sichuan cookbooks existed in English at the time.

• **Her favourite mooncakes are savoury**, particularly Shanghai-style minced pork mooncakes and Yunnan varieties such as flaky pastry stuffed with Yunnan ham and sugar, or larger Weishan mooncakes with red bean or rose petal fillings—rather than the more commonly known rich Cantonese-style lotus seed paste versions.

articles.title: Kurt Campbell on US deterrence, the Quad, Aukus and Taiwan after Xi-Trump summit
articles.summary:
Here is the summary:

- **Kurt Campbell's background**: Campbell served as White House coordinator for Indo-Pacific affairs (2021–2024) and US deputy secretary of state (2024–2025), and was a key architect of the Obama administration's "pivot to Asia," the Quad, and the "small yard, high fence" technology strategy toward China.

- **Post-summit stabilization**: Campbell acknowledges that both US and Chinese leaders have determined it is in both countries' interests to stabilize the complex bilateral relationship, driven by a mix of competitive positioning and genuine cooperation.

- **Concerns about US allied relationships**: Campbell warns that President Trump has prioritized the US-China relationship at the expense of key allies and partners, citing deteriorating US-Canada relations as "shocking" and expressing alarm over Canada's interest in joining the EU.

- **Core argument on US strategy**: Campbell maintains that US global effectiveness depends on working constructively with allies and partners, arguing that stabilizing the US-China relationship alone is insufficient without simultaneously maintaining a strong allied posture and broader partnerships.

articles.title: Hong Kong’s historic vessels sail into the future
articles.summary:
- **Way Foong**, a wooden motoryacht built in 1930 by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company for HSBC, served the bank as a ferry, tugboat, and pleasure craft for over 70 years before entering private ownership and later being acquired by the Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF).

- **Java**, another 1930s wooden vessel from the same shipyard (entered service 1935), served in the Hong Kong government fleet as Marine 1, performing VIP transport, anti-piracy patrols, and buoy positioning. Its Burmese-teak construction earned it a reputation as "almost unsinkable."

- The HKHVF, founded earlier this year, currently owns and maintains **five historic vessels**. Historians have identified **nine extant pre-1950s Hong Kong-built boats** in total, with one, **Mon Lei**, whose whereabouts remain unknown.

- The foundation's CEO, Philip Giannecchini, states its mission is to preserve Hong Kong's maritime heritage, showcase local shipyard craftsmanship, and foster the next generation of boaters and ocean-lovers in the region.

articles.title: Southeast Asia battles Big Tech to protect children online
articles.summary:
- **Indonesia enacted strict regulations in March barring under-16s from "high-risk" social media platforms, but underage users continue to circumvent the rules by lying about their age, highlighting the limits of age-verification systems.**

- **Big Tech companies have complied to varying degrees: TikTok raised its minimum age to 16 on March 28 and deactivated 9 million underage accounts by October; Meta raised the minimum age to 16 in April; Roblox began face-scanning Indonesian users for age estimation.**

- **Indonesia's government has given tech companies until year-end to complete self-assessments of their age-verification, algorithmic, and ad-targeting systems; non-compliance could result in fines of up to 6% of global revenue — roughly US$12 billion if applied to Meta's reported 2025 revenue.**

- **This approach mirrors broader global accountability for Big Tech: Meta agreed in August to pay up to US$18 billion to settle US state lawsuits alleging its platforms were designed to addict children, with sweeping changes to teen usage controls mandated as a result.**

articles.title: From fishing boats to Michelin stars: Vietnam’s CoCo Dining turns the humble into haute cuisine
articles.summary:
- Chef Vo Thanh Vuong, founder of CoCo Dining, grew up fishing off Vietnam's coast after his family's boat sank in 2000 when he was 11, leaving him to fish full-time until age 20 before moving to Ho Chi Minh City.

- He operates a restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City and frequently returns to Vung Tau — the port city that supplies the city's best restaurants — to fish, source ingredients, and draw on his deep connection to the sea.

- His cooking philosophy is rooted in simplicity and respect for ingredients: "When an ingredient is truly good, you don't need to do much to it. Sometimes, the best thing a cook can do is step out of the way."

- His preparations showcase fresh seafood with straightforward techniques — steaming flower crabs and swimming crabs with beer, making a tamarind-pineapple-tomato hotpot, and curing thin slices of oriental trumpeter whiting in lime juice — blending the speed of a fisherman's cooking with the deliberate craft of a chef.

articles.title: Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
articles.summary:
- **Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory is a major global export hub**: The Lingang factory assembles a Model Y L in under 40 seconds, and in July 2025 set a record by shipping 7,738 vehicles in a single roll-on/roll-off vessel from a Chinese port. It delivered 93,579 vehicles that month, with over half of this year's production exported overseas.

- **Geopolitical tensions create a dilemma for Elon Musk**: Tesla relies heavily on China's supply chain for global EV demand, while SpaceX serves as a key US Pentagon national-security contractor, placing Musk in a difficult position between Washington and Beijing.

- **Speculation about a Tesla-SpaceX merger is growing**: Increasing technology overlap—from AI to robotics—has fueled merger talk, though Musk has neither confirmed nor denied it. Morningstar's Seth Goldstein notes the two companies "are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another," with Tesla providing solar panels, batteries, and potential Starship cargo casings, and SpaceX offering its Grok AI model and Starlink internet for Tesla products.

- **Experts warn of mounting geopolitical risk**: Marina Yue Zhang of the Australia-China Relations Institute says Musk is currently balancing multiple business tracks rather than choosing sides, but maintaining this balance is increasingly dangerous given the uncertain geopolitical landscape, and could intensify significantly if the businesses were formally merged.

articles.title: Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
articles.summary:
- Tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of Thailand's economy; visitor numbers fell from a record ~30 million in 2019 to 32.9 million in 2024, with the government trimming its 2026 forecast to 30–34 million due to rising oil prices, higher airfares, and geopolitical conflicts (Ukraine war, US-Israel-Iran tensions).

- The post-Covid tourism landscape has shifted from mass bus-tour groups to "free, independent tourists" (FITs), reducing foot traffic at traditional group-oriented attractions like the Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm.

- A strong Thai baht has made Thailand less competitive on price, pushing budget-conscious travelers toward cheaper alternatives in Vietnam and Malaysia.

- Despite a 60-day visa-free scheme introduced in 2024 to attract visitors, arrivals remain below pre-pandemic peaks, and the article suggests that growing frustration with foreign tourist misbehavior is further straining the industry's appeal.

articles.title: Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving
articles.summary:
- **Surging costs are driving car owners off Singapore's roads.** Certificate of Entitlement (COE) renewal prices have skyrocketed—from S$10,000 in 2006 to over S$112,000 in 2024—combined with rising road tax, fuel, maintenance, insurance, and congestion charges (ERP), pushing more Singaporeans to abandon private car ownership.

- **Private car numbers hit a five-year low.** Government figures from July show 516,237 privately owned cars in Singapore, the lowest since 2019, though they still make up 79% of all vehicles on the road; rental, ride-hailing, and corporate vehicles have grown as a share.

- **Singapore's government is actively promoting a "car-lite" society.** The Land Transport Authority's "Move Lite" campaign, launched in 2022, encourages walking, cycling, and public transport use—shifting from highlighting public transport benefits to spotlighting the downsides of driving, such as congestion and parking hassles.

- **ERP congestion charges are being expanded.** Electronic road pricing charges returned to the Orchard Road shopping district at the start of September 2024, the first reintroduction since the pandemic began in 2020, as part of broader demand-management measures.

- **Infrastructure investment underpins the strategy.** Singapore continues investing in public transport and "active mobility" infrastructure while managing vehicle ownership and road usage to balance competing needs within its land constraints and ensure sustainable, efficient transport for all road users.

articles.title: Chinese brokers work to crack the final code: win clients on global stage
articles.summary:
• **China's capital market ambitions have evolved**: Beijing's goal has shifted from emulating Goldman Sachs to building first-class investment institutions with distinct Chinese characteristics, as called for by President Xi Jinping at the 2023 Central Financial Work Conference. China now operates the world's second-largest capital market after the US.

• **A major structural shift in financing**: In 2025, direct financing through stocks and bonds surpassed bank lending for the first time, signaling a "golden era" for Chinese securities firms.

• **Expansion beyond mainland China is the next frontier**: With Hong Kong's role expanding and mainland companies investing more aggressively overseas, Chinese brokerages are increasingly pushing into international markets. Overseas business, particularly in Hong Kong, is identified as a key growth driver by Fitch Ratings.

• **From apprentices to competitors**: Chinese investment banks spent decades learning from Wall Street—beginning with the 1995 founding of CICC, whose executives studied Western markets under Morgan Stanley's guidance. China Mobile's 1997 US$4.2 billion dual listing was an early milestone. Over two decades, Chinese firms evolved from learning basic mechanics to acquiring the networks and capabilities needed to compete internationally.

articles.title: The AI promise was automation. The reality? Managing digital workers
articles.summary:
- **AI agents in Asia are proving more burdensome than expected**: Instead of eliminating corporate drudgery, autonomous AI agents are creating additional management layers, communication overhead, and bureaucratic friction — as illustrated by a Shanghai-based product marketer whose AI agents became deadlocked debating task ownership and responsibilities.

- **Rapid adoption across the region and globally**: Meta's personal agent Muse reached an estimated 2.8 million downloads in two weeks; the open-source agent OpenClaw triggered a "raising lobsters" craze in mainland China, with hundreds queuing outside Tencent's Shenzhen headquarters for installation help; and major tech firms like Tencent, Alibaba, and Baidu have launched agent-focused enterprise products.

- **A gap between AI capability and organizational readiness**: Businesses from Singaporean hotels to Hong Kong's service sector report that straightforward workflows become complex puzzles when delegated to agents, as they struggle to navigate fragmented systems, multi-departmental processes, and determine when human intervention is needed.

articles.title: Why did Hong Kong’s 11 Skies fail and can the megaproject be rescued?
articles.summary:
- **11 Skies, a 3.8 million-square-foot commercial complex at Hong Kong International Airport, has largely failed**, with minimal footfall, mostly dark and unoccupied retail and office spaces, and only one of three office towers partially occupied.

- **New World Development surrendered its nearly 50-year contract** for the project in October, paying a HK$2.3 billion break-up fee plus an additional HK$1.05 billion for works and services, amid its ongoing debt crisis since 2023. The Airport Authority will resume control and plans to rebrand the project as an entertainment hub.

- **The Airport Authority holds a call option** to buy 750 million New World shares at HK$3 each from majority shareholder Chow Tai Fook Enterprises within three years, though the conditions attached raise questions about its feasibility.

- **The break-up raises concerns about moral hazard**, as analysts note it could affect developers' ex ante incentives in future public projects, though experts caution that the negotiated termination with substantial payments differs from an unconditional exit and should not be easily characterized as a developer returning a project "at will."
